title: Canonical vector factor of a smooth commutative p-torsion group
statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, with $p$ prime [def-weil-field]. Groups are affine $k$-group schemes of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], and smooth and connected mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Write $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$ [def-sc-gm-ga] and $\mathbb A^1_k=\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-polynomial-ring]. A smooth connected unipotent $k$-group is called $k$-wound if every $k$-scheme morphism $\mathbb A^1_k\to H$ is constant with value in $H(k)$. Here unipotent means having a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation with unipotent geometric points. The condition $[p]_H=0$ for a commutative group means that on every commutative $k$-algebra the sum of $p$ copies of each section is zero. Let $H$ be smooth, connected and commutative with $[p]_H=0$, and fix a separable closure $k_s/k$. There exist smooth connected closed subgroups $V,W\subseteq H$ and an integer $d\geq0$ such that multiplication $V\times_k W\to H$ is an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes, $V\simeq\mathbf G_a^d$, and $W_{k_s}$ is $k_s$-wound. The subgroup $V$ is unique among such decompositions. More precisely, $V_{k_s}$ is the smallest closed subgroup of $H_{k_s}$ through which every $k_s$-scheme morphism $\mathbb A^1_{k_s}\to H_{k_s}$ taking $0$ to the identity factors. One has $V=1$ if and only if $H$ is $k$-wound. The complement $W$ need not be unique. The trivial group and $d=0$ are allowed, and $k$ need not be perfect.

source.place: Brian Conrad, The structure of solvable groups over general fields (2014), Definition 2.1, printed p.10; Theorem 2.6 and its proof, printed pp.12--13; Corollary 2.7, printed p.13. Read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf. WANTED locally: this document. No Stacks tag is claimed for this Tits structure theorem.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-p-torsion-additive-embedding] to $H$: it is a smooth commutative affine $k$-group scheme of finite type with $[p]_H=0$, exactly the hypotheses of that lemma (connectedness and perfectness of $k$ are not needed there). It gives $N\geq0$ and a homomorphism $H\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_a^N$ identifying $H$ with a closed subgroup scheme; identify $H$ with this closed subgroup of $E=\mathbf G_a^N$.

source.place: Theorem 2.6, printed p.12, invocation of Lemma 1.14.

proof.text: Take $K=k_s$ and the family of all pointed $K$-scheme morphisms $\mathbb A^1_K\to H_K$. Conjugating coefficients by any element of $\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)$ gives another member of the same family. Thus [lem-sfb-galois-stable-affine-line-generated-subgroup] gives a smooth connected closed $k$-subgroup $V\subseteq H$ whose extension $V_K$ is their smallest containing closed subgroup. This is the required generation property, not just a statement about $K$-points.

source.place: Theorem 2.6, first sentence of proof, printed p.12.

proof.text: Inside $E_K$, the same family generates $V_K$: a closed subgroup of $E_K$ containing it intersects $H_K$ in a closed subgroup of $H_K$ containing it, hence contains $V_K$. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-line-generated-vector-subgroup-straightening] to $V\subseteq E$. It yields $V\simeq\mathbf G_a^d$ and a homomorphic retraction $r:E\to V$. Restrict it to $H$. Put $W=\ker(r|_H)$; in straightened coordinates it is the closed intersection $H\cap(\{0\}^d\times\mathbf G_a^{N-d})$. The mutually inverse morphisms are $(v,w)\mapsto v+w$ and $x\mapsto(r(x),x-r(x))$. The latter lands in $V\times W$ since $r(x-r(x))=r(x)-r(x)=0$. These identities hold on every $k$-algebra, giving the group-scheme product decomposition over $k$.

source.place: Theorem 2.6, printed p.12, Proposition 1.15 and Corollary 1.16; explicit retraction-kernel argument for the latter.

proof.text: The projection $q:H\to W$, $x\mapsto x-r(x)$, has the inclusion $i:W\to H$ as a section. Thus $W$ is connected: $q$ is a continuous surjection from connected $H$. It is affine finite type since it is the closed coordinate intersection above. The scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is locally Noetherian (a field has only the two ideals), so [pqf-lem-lft-fp-locnoeth] gives local finite presentation of $W\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. For any first order affine thickening $T\subset T'$ and $a:T\to W$, smoothness of $H$, in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], lifts $ia$ to $b:T'\to H$; then $qb$ lifts $a$ because $qi=1_W$. The same definition therefore gives smoothness of $W$.

source.place: Theorem 2.6, printed p.12, direct-factor smoothness and connectedness; smoothness expanded using the existing infinitesimal definition and finite-presentation leaf.

proof.text: Both $H$ and $W$ are unipotent in the stated sense: restrict the faithful representation of $E$ which sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_N)$ to the $(N+1)$ by $(N+1)$ identity matrix with those entries in the rest of its first row. Its difference from the identity has square zero, and its entries recover every $a_i$ on every algebra. To check woundness, translate any $f:\mathbb A^1_K\to W_K$ by $-f(0)$ to make it pointed. Its composite with $W_K\hookrightarrow H_K$ factors through $V_K$ by step 2, so factors through $V_K\cap W_K=1$ by step 3. Thus the translated map is zero and $f$ is constant with value $f(0)\in W(K)$.

source.place: Theorem 2.6, last sentence on printed p.12; Definition 2.1, translation criterion, printed p.10.

proof.text: Given another such decomposition $H=V'\times W'$, every pointed affine-line map into $H_K$ projects to zero in the wound group $W'_K$. Minimality from step 2 gives $V_K\subseteq V'_K$. Conversely, each coordinate axis $\mathbf G_{a,K}\to V'_K\simeq\mathbf G_{a,K}^{d'}\hookrightarrow H_K$ is a pointed affine-line map, hence factors through $V_K$; adding the axes shows $V'_K\subseteq V_K$. These subgroup inclusions descend to $k$: for their defining ideals, an inclusion can be tested after tensoring with the field extension $K/k$, since a $k$-vector space injects into its scalar extension. Consequently $V'=V$.

source.place: Theorem 2.6, uniqueness argument, printed p.13, using coordinate axes for its reverse inclusion.

proof.text: If $V=1$, the product identifies $H_K$ with the wound group $W_K$. Any pointed $k$-affine-line map to $H$ becomes zero over $K$, hence is already zero: equality of coordinate-algebra maps is detected by the injective scalar extension $k[x]\to K[x]$. Translation gives that every map is constant. Conversely, if $d>0$, a coordinate axis in $V\simeq\mathbf G_a^d$ followed by its inclusion in $H$ is nonconstant, so a wound $H$ forces $d=0$. The zero-dimensional vector group and trivial $H$ cause no exception. Uniqueness concerns $V$: for any homomorphism $a:W\to V$, the graph $w\mapsto(a(w),w)$ is another complement, with product inverse $(v,w)\mapsto(v-a(w),w)$. Thus the decomposition makes no assertion of uniqueness for $W$.

source.place: Corollary 2.7 and the remark following Theorem 2.6, printed p.13.

proof_origin.place: Online Conrad Theorem 2.6 proof, printed pp.12--13, Corollary 2.7 and Definition 2.1; the PDF is WANTED locally. Assembly and explicit coordinate/retraction details written by Q80 after reading the online source.
